Title: Deep Learning-based Concept Detection in vitrivr at the Video Browser Showdown 2019 – Final Notes
Text:
Deep Learning-based Concept Detection in vitrivr at the Video
Browser Showdown 2019 – Final Notes
Luca Rosseto1, Mahnaz Amiri Parian1,2, Ralph Gasser1, Ivan Giangreco1,
Silvan Heller1, Heiko Schuldt1
1Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Basel, Switzerland
2Numediart Institute, University of Mons, Belgium
{ﬁrstname.lastname}@unibas.ch
ABSTRACT
Tis paper presents an afer-the-fact summary of the participation
of the vitrivr system [8] to the 2019 Video Browser Showdown [1].
Analogously to last year’s report [5], the focus of this paper lies on
additions made since the original publication [10] and the system’s
performance during the competition.
1
INTRODUCTION
vitrivr is an open-source multimedia retrieval stack which has –
together which its predecessor, the IMOTION system – participated
in the VBS ﬁve times so far [4, 6, 7, 9, 10] and was ranked 1st for the
second time this year afer it had already won the 2017 installment
of the competition.
Tis paper provides an addendum to the original publication [10]
by describing the additions made to the system that lacked docu-
mentation (Section 2). Furthermore, we discuss the system’s over-
all performance during the competition (Section 3) as well as the
lessons we have learned (Section 4).
2
ADDITIONS
Tis section provides an overview of the additions that were made
afer the submission of the original publication [10]. Tese addi-
tions were mostly concerned with eﬃciency and ease-of-use in a
competitive seting such as VBS.
2.1
Feature Extraction
As mentioned in the original paper, we made use of various methods
to extract or generate textual descriptions from the video content.
In order to label actions that were performed during a video shot,
we used the Inﬂated 3D Convolution I3D1 network pretrained on
the Kinetics 6002 dataset [2], which covers 600 diﬀerent actions.
Since the new dataset [11], in contrast to the previous one, does
not include any ASR data, we generated the speech transcripts for
the videos containing English dialogue using the Google Cloud
Speech-to-Text API3.
2.2
Collaborative Retrieval
Since the setup during the competition called for two independent
instances of the retrieval system, operated by one user each, we
implemented a small coordination utility4 in order to facilitate
collaborative retrieval. Te user interface already had the option

to highlight speciﬁc results with a user-deﬁnable color. In the
new version, a result that has been submited to the competition
server would now also automatically be assigned a color. Figure 1
depicts an example of a submited result in red. Te coordination
utility shares these color labels across several instances of the user
interface, so one user can see what the other has already labeled
or submited. Tis functionality turned out to be especially useful
during the Ad-hoc Video Search (AVS) tasks, since it greatly reduced
redundancies in submited results and did therefore allow for a more
eﬃcient use of the limited time available.
2.3
Improvements of Interaction Eﬃciency
In order to make the interaction with the system more eﬃcient in
a competitive seting, we made several minor improvements to the
user interface which are brieﬂy described as follows:
• Te Qery by Sketch input was amended by a palete of
frequently-used colors such as various skin tones.
• An additional ﬁlter step was added to remove retrieved
results from the user interface. Filtering is possible by score,
so as to exclude results below a certain score threshold, and
by dominant color of a shot. Te later does for example
enable the user to only show results that are predominantly
‘orange’ or ‘yellow’ in hue.
• Since we greatly increased the number of returned results,
the display logic of the user interface was changed such
that it would load the preview images on demand rather
than all at once in order not to overly stress the browser
running the UI. Additional optimizations were also made
to beter cope with the greatly enlarged result set.
• Te user interface does now store the results from all previ-
ous queries. A dedicated menu lists the entire query history
and allows a user to load any previous result without gen-
erating load on the retrieval back-end. Te idea behind
this was that in a competitive seting, the user should be
able to go back to a successful query afer having issued
an unsuccessful one.
• We added the option to submit an item by holding down the
‘Shif’-key and clicking on it. Normally, clicking the result
would open the retrieved video at the relevant point in time.
Tis simple change improved the submission eﬃciency
dramatically, especially during Ad-hoc Video Search (AVS)
tasks. In previous versions, this functionality was hidden
in a dedicated menu that would only appear when hovering
a result item with the mouse.

3
SYSTEM USE AND PERFORMANCE
Even though vitrivr oﬀers several diﬀerent query modalities, both
expert and novice users used text-based queries almost exclusively.
Tis is not surprising, since in a time-constrained seting, textual
input is quicker to produce than the visual alternatives. Especially
for queries that contained either suﬃcient dialog or clearly visual
text on screen, textual queries in the corresponding categories
proved not only eﬃcient but also highly eﬀective. In the absence
of such cues, the large number of labelled concepts and actions as
well as the scene captions provided ample basis for textual search.
In this iteration of the competition, vitrivr performed well in all
task categories. Out of the ﬁve, it was ranked ﬁrst in three of them
and was only outranked by the VIRET [3] system in the other two.
Te overall placements for the diﬀerent task types were as follows:
• 2nd place in textual KIS tasks (80/100 points)
• 1st place in visual expert KIS tasks (100/100 points)
• 1st place in novice visual KIS tasks (100/100 points)
• 2nd place in expert AVS tasks (76/100 points)
• 1st place in novice AVS tasks (100/100 points)
• 1st place overall (91/100)
4
LESSONS LEARNED
In the following, we summarize some of the observations made
during the competition:
• Text is still a very eﬀective and intuitive way to specify
queries, especially for novice users.
• Visual Qery-by-Sketch is not suﬃciently selective for
a collection of the size that is currently in use and does
therefore (at least in a competitive seting) not justify the
time required for query formulation and execution.
• Te semantic sketch queries look promising but their exe-
cution time needs to be reduced in order to be useful in a
competitive seting.
• In a time-constrained seting, browsing through a larger
result set is more eﬀective than trying to make the query
more precise in order to reduce that set.
• Despite its eﬀectiveness, browsing can still lead to false-
negatives as did happen in the 9th visual Known-Item
Search (KIS) task, where the correct result was retrieved
by the system but overlooked by both users.
• For Ad-hoc Video Search (AVS) tasks, eﬃcient submission
is just as important as eﬀective retrieval. Te added short-
cuts for submission as well as the result synchronization
were very helpful in that respect.
5
CONCLUSION
While vitrivr performed well in this edition of the Video Browser
Showdown, there remain several improvements to be made. Large-
scale video search is far from being a solved problem and variability
in the outcomes of VBS over recent years show that in such a
competitive seting, the ﬁnal results are not an absolute measure
for one system’s performance with respect to another. Creativity in
query formulation and to a certain degree plain luck also inﬂuence
the ﬁnal ranking of the systems.
